editorNote: A winter week of games, home computers and music-making.
morningLine: Nintendo offers a fresh vision for home play; the computer makers sharpen their pitches.

lead.headline: Nintendo puts games at the heart of its Advanced Video System
lead.dek: January’s winter show offers a game machine with a home-computing ambition.
body: Nintendo’s Advanced Video System offers a striking proposal for the living room: a sleek game unit that can be joined by an optional keyboard and tape-drive accessories. Demonstrated at the January 5–8 Winter Consumer Electronics Show in Las Vegas, the design remains one of the month’s notable consumer-computing talking points.

The publicity folder presents more than a stand-alone toy. Its accessories suggest a path from games toward home computing, placing familiar game play and the promise of a keyboard within the same design. This is a show presentation, however, rather than an American retail launch.

For buyers, the unanswered questions are practical ones. A verified retail price and shipping date are not established by the preserved presentation material. A display floor can show what a manufacturer wants to build; it cannot by itself tell a family when the machine will be available at the local store.

Against the new Atari and Commodore proposals, Nintendo’s emphasis gives games their own place in the winter conversation. The Advanced Video System is the name on this January proposal, and its optional computing accessories are part of that proposal—not proof that a complete system is already on sale.

stories.headline: Atari challenges Macintosh prices with the ST
stories.dek: A lower announced price still demands a new software library.
body: Atari’s January CES announcement puts the ST family in an announced $400–$600 price range. The Motorola MC68000 processor also powers Macintosh, but sharing a processor does not make the machines compatible with one another’s software. The figures describe announced computers, not verified complete retail packages.

Sigmund Hartmann has promised 25–30 software products by the time the computers reach stores. Electronic Arts president Trip Hawkins estimated that 30–50 percent of a Macintosh program might require reworking for the ST. The low-price challenge therefore depends on programmers as well as hardware.

Jack Tramiel is making an ambitious bid with constrained finances: the January 8 report says Atari lacks a bank line of credit, while Tramiel has set a $1 billion sales goal for 1985. Those are reported conditions and a target, not results already achieved.

stories.headline: Commodore 128 offers three paths from one keyboard
stories.dek: Compatibility is the winter pitch to existing C64 owners.
body: Commodore’s January show machine combines a C64-compatible mode with a 128K mode and a Z80-based CP/M mode. The January 8 newspaper account confirms a computer with twice the C64’s memory; the detailed configuration is documented in later reporting on the winter presentation.

BASIC 7.0 adds sound, graphics and disk commands in 128 mode, while C64 mode retains BASIC 2.0. The new mode offers a choice of 40- or 80-column displays; that 80-column option does not belong to C64 mode. A separate numeric keypad helps distinguish the 92-key keyboard.

An under-$300 indication and a spring introduction schedule should not be mistaken for an official show price or accomplished availability. For the C64 owner, the central attraction is a proposed upgrade path that preserves a familiar mode while opening other uses.

stories.headline: Rails West! and Questron take the long route
stories.dek: January’s software shelf offers finance and fantasy.
body: SSI’s January magazine announcement offers two ways to spend an evening far from arcade reflexes. Rails West! models late-nineteenth-century American railway development for as many as eight players, making corporations and capital as important as tracks.

Players can found or take over companies, trade stocks and bonds, seek loans and float securities. Booms and panics alter the financial landscape. Apple, Atari and Commodore 64 disk editions are advertised at $39.95.

Questron sends the player against Wizard Mantor to recover the Book of Evil Magic and save an empire. Its advertised disk prices are $39.95 for C64 and $49.95 for Apple or Atari. The January listing is a period shelf announcement, not evidence that either game first appeared during this particular week.

worldAnchor.headline: Brazil elects a civilian president after 21 years
worldAnchor.summary: On January 15, Tancredo Neves won the Electoral College vote, 480 to 180 over Paulo Maluf. His inauguration is scheduled for March 15.

gadgetWatch.headline: Sony plans a sharp jump in CD-player production
gadgetWatch.summary: Billboard January 19, page 3, reports Sony’s plan to increase production from around 150,000 players in 1984 to a projected 700,000 in 1985, with roughly half destined for Japan and half Europe/US. A forecast, not achieved output.

bbsNote.headline: 2400-bps ambitions run ahead of commercial access
bbsNote.summary: January’s telecomputing column places hobbyist bulletin boards ahead of commercial services in the race toward 2400 bps.

posts.text: The column reports seed-program talks offering selected sysops 2400-bps modems near 1200-bps prices; no named board or confirmed rollout date.

posts.platform: CompuServe / The Source / Delphi / Dow Jones News/Retrieval
posts.text: January publication says these services do not yet offer 2400 bps; verify any later change before stating it as a January 20 fact.

curiosity.headline: A home computer can straighten a musician’s rhythm
curiosity.summary: The $225 Sequential Circuits package turns a C64 into a six-track MIDI sequencer.
curiosity.detail: Richard Mansfield describes adjustable Autocorrection ranging from quarter-note to thirty-second-triplet resolution, letting players choose how tightly the computer moves notes onto the beat. This is a January review, not a release this week.

periodAd.headline: Sequential Circuits: six tracks at the keyboard
periodAd.summary: The $225 C64 MIDI Music Sequencer offers six editable tracks and eight chainable sequences, with tape or disk storage.

market.headline: Speed has a price—and needs a destination
market.summary: January’s modem column quotes $50–$280 for 300 bps and $800–$1,500 for 2400 bps. CompuServe, The Source, Delphi and Dow Jones News/Retrieval were not yet offering 2400-bps access at publication; a faster modem alone cannot accelerate every service.

items: No milestone designated: CES launches were January 5–8, outside this issue week; do not announce them as January 14–20 events.
April COMPUTE! CES reporting is explicitly retrospective; contemporaneous January 8 Times is the main Atari source.
Billboard is the actual January 19 Top Rock Tracks chart, not Tunecaster’s different weekly ranking. Primary PDF text verifies top five.
Underground check found no adequately dated January scene story or named crews; omit beat rather than repurpose February piracy television or November Phrack.
Game Entertainer January PDF was located but scanned text could not be extracted; OCR executable unavailable. No detailed claims imported from it.
Complete means a usable sourced dossier, not an exhaustive archive survey; exact-week computer product news remains thin.
Five game shelf selections are editorial picks, not ranked sales. Two additional titles use April retrospective coverage of January CES.
The Nintendo gaming proposal is the visual and editorial lead; all CES material is explicitly same-month aftermath.
